executive_summary: SGD/CHF closed at 0.64492 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in Swiss francs per Singapore dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger Singapore dollar. The pair fell 0.63% over the past month after rising 2.22% over three months and 4.84% over six months. It sits at the 81st percentile of its 52-week closing range (0.60555-0.65408) and 27 pips below a 200-week average of 0.64765 that it has not closed above for 127 weeks. The pair weighs two things against each other. Holding the Singapore dollar against the franc pays about 130bp a year in money-market carry (three-month SORA at 1.297% against an SNB rate of 0%). Against that, the franc's safe-haven role came back in October when French sovereign stress pushed the OAT-Bund spread to 152.5bp, and the Singapore dollar has no matching haven bid. Each dossier is strategically Bullish on its own currency for the same reasons: a large external surplus, a credible hawkish-leaning central bank and AAA public finances. In this cross those strengths cancel. That leaves carry set against Swiss policy risk at the 10 December SNB assessment and the haven tail. The tactical stance is Neutral (score +0.053, conviction 2, confidence 51%). The strategic stance is Neutral (score +0.014, conviction 1, confidence 49%). The expected outcome is a range in which carry of about 7 pips a month is the main source of return. Downside tails are larger than upside tails, because the franc's haven bid hits this pair directly while resistance bands and the 200-week average sit just above spot. The main caveat is that no option or future on the Singapore dollar is listed anywhere. Implied volatility, skew and market forwards for this cross cannot be observed. Every forward figure here is derived from the rate gap, and any position has to be built through the USD/SGD and USD/CHF legs.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Real effective rates point in opposite directions for the two currencies. The BIS real broad index for SGD was 115.04 in September, the 88th percentile of its readings since January 2024 and the second-highest in the G10+SGD set. The CHF real index was 98.37, the lowest of its 33 monthly readings over the same period. On recent history, then, the Singapore dollar is rich and the franc cheap, which is a slow-moving valuation headwind for the pair. World Bank GDP-based PPP says the opposite: it puts the Singapore dollar about 45% below parity against the franc, with an implied SGD/CHF of 1.1768. That gap reflects Singapore's low measured price level and has not closed in decades, so neither dossier treats it as actionable. At 0.64492 the pair prices a franc that is still a carry-funding currency with a revived but contained haven role. It does not price a hawkish SNB forecast or a structural re-rating of either real exchange rate.

market_context.recent_regime: From May to September the pair traded as a franc-funded carry cross. The SNB held at 0% while peers hiked, and the franc's haven appeal had faded after the SNB's March intervention, so SGD/CHF rose 6.9% from 0.61183 to 0.65408. Rabobank noted in September that, measured from the start of the Iran war, the franc was the second-worst G10 performer after the krona, raising the prospect of it becoming a funding currency. October broke the regime. French fiscal stress revived the franc's haven role, and the 1 October outside reversal from 0.65500 was followed by a 0.71% fall on 15 October around the MAS hold and a low close of 0.64249 on 22 October. The month ended with the pair pinned between the six-touch resistance band and the 50-day average, a 27-pip gap from the 200-week average, and the dominant narrative split between carry and haven.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry is +129.7bp to a long SGD/CHF position. This is three-month compounded SORA (1.297%, 30 October) minus the SNB policy rate (0%); Singapore has no policy rate, so SORA stands in as the base short rate in base_policy_rate. It is a money-market gap, not a forward-implied funding gap. No Singapore dollar future or listed forward exists, so the true cost of carry, including any cross-currency basis, cannot be observed. Ten-year yields point the same way: SGS 2.24% against the Swiss ten-year at 0.47% (both 30 October daily closes) is a +177bp gap, or about +165bp on the September monthly Swiss average of 0.59%. Carry is worth about 84 pips a year at 0.64492: roughly 7 pips a month, 21 pips over three months and 42 over six months. The carry-to-implied-volatility ratio cannot be calculated because no implied volatility exists, so it is null. On realised volatility alone, carry is 0.25 times 60-day realised (5.12%) and 0.27 times 20-day realised (4.78%); these are realised-volatility measures, not the framework's implied-volatility ratio. The Singapore dollar dossier puts the same realised-based ratio at +0.25 and calls this SGD's only clearly positive carry trade.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Singapore has no policy rate, so the rate comparison has to use money markets. Three-month compounded SORA was 1.297% on 30 October. The SNB policy rate is 0%, held on 24 September. That gives the Singapore dollar a yield advantage of about 130bp, its only clearly positive carry against a G10 currency. Ten-year yields point the same way. SGS yielded 2.24% on 30 October and the Swiss ten-year 0.47% on the same day (the September monthly average was 0.59%), a gap of roughly 165-177bp. Over four weeks the gap should hold steady or widen slightly. SORA has risen from a second-quarter average of 1.06% as US rates fed through, and a 9 December Fed hike is about 77% priced. The SNB's next decision on the confirmed calendar is 10 December, outside this window. No MAS decision falls in the window either, and the October statement left the band unchanged. With nothing scheduled to reprice either side for four weeks, the gap simply pays holders of the pair. That is a real but small support: 130bp a year is about 7 pips a month at the 30 October rate of 0.64492.

We agree on both, so the tactical support comes from carry earned, not from a repricing. A hot Swiss CPI on 3 November is the only near-term way the gap could narrow.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the rate gap meets its first scheduled test at the SNB's quarterly assessment on 10 December. That is the only decision on the confirmed calendar for either currency before March. The SNB's September conditional forecast had inflation at 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027 with the rate at 0%. Both dossiers put the chance of an unchanged rate in December at about 85%, so the base case is that the zero rate lasts through the horizon. On the Singapore side, the money-market rate follows from the exchange-rate regime rather than being set directly. If the Fed hikes on 9 December, SORA should drift a little higher through the forward market and widen the gap modestly. The risks both run towards a narrower gap. A hawkish SNB forecast or a hint of a 2027 hike would narrow it from the Swiss side. A flatter MAS slope, which the Singapore dossier gives a 10% chance, would weaken the Singapore side. On balance the gap most likely stays around 130-150bp through February, keeping carry in the Singapore dollar's favour. Confidence is lower than tactically because a dated Swiss repricing event now falls inside the horizon.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Singapore has both the stronger growth and the firmer inflation. Third-quarter GDP rose 5.4% y/y against Swiss growth of about 2.6% y/y. MAS core inflation is 2.0%, against Swiss core CPI of 0.5% and headline of 1.0%. These gaps move the pair through each central bank's reaction, not directly. Singapore's strength (NODX up 68.4% y/y in September, unemployment at 2.0%) removes any case for a flatter MAS slope. That keeps the S$NEER rising against its basket, which includes the franc. Swiss momentum is softening: the KOF barometer fell to 107.6 in October from 109.1, the procure.ch PMI fell to 55.3, and nominal wage growth is only 0.4%. None of that argues for an early SNB move. The release that matters most for the pair is Swiss October CPI on 3 November. A print of 1.2% or more would revive SNB hike pricing and push the pair down, but the CHF dossier expects 1.0-1.1%, close to pricing. Singapore's October NODX and CPI arrive in the second half of November and are more likely to confirm strength than to disappoint. On balance the data lean towards the Singapore dollar, with modest confidence because the MAS band limits how far Singapore data move its currency.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the policy relevance of the data shifts. In Singapore, MAS expects the positive output gap to narrow through 2027 and core inflation to ease noticeably from mid-2027. Export growth also faces a very high base as the AI-driven surge laps itself, so Singapore's data stop pushing MAS towards a steeper slope. In Switzerland, the SNB's forecast has inflation rising further in the fourth quarter, and Brent above US$115 puts the CHF dossier's early-2027 headline risk at 1.2-1.5%. That would give the SNB a reason to tighten from the lowest inflation base in the group. Against this, Swiss growth faces the slowdown SECO expects after a pharma-driven second quarter. Singapore keeps the better growth-inflation mix, which keeps MAS biased towards tightening. Rising Swiss inflation is the one channel through which the data could narrow the rate gap. The two effects roughly cancel, so the factor carries no directional weight at this horizon.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: The pair sets a classic haven (CHF) against a low-beta, trade-weighted currency (SGD), so risk sentiment reaches the pair almost entirely through the franc. That asymmetry warrants more weight than the default, funded by the reduced dollar-funding weight on a non-USD cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Risk sentiment reaches this pair mainly through the franc. October showed how: French sovereign stress took the OAT-Bund spread to 152.5bp after a high near 159bp, the widest since 2011. The franc gained against the euro, and the Singapore dollar has no comparable European exposure. Broader gauges are softening rather than breaking. The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October and touched 20.05 intraday the next day, and US high-yield spreads were 18bp wider at 326bp. In a wider risk-off, the Singapore dollar weakens against the US dollar within its band while the franc tends to gain, so the pair falls in a European stress and in a global one. There are offsets. Equities remain firm, with the SMI up 8.72% in October. Gold, which usually moves with the franc, fell about 7% in October, removing one supporting signal. We lean Bearish with modest confidence: the haven bid is active, the Singapore dollar's low beta does not shield it against a haven currency, and the tail risks fall in the next four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk outlook could go either way. French borrowing costs near 24-year highs and a negative Moody's outlook keep the euro-sovereign tail alive, and the Middle East war is in its ninth month. Either escalation would favour the franc over the Singapore dollar. Against that, Qatari mediation makes a ceasefire a real possibility. A ceasefire would cut oil and help Asian importers, Singapore among them, while reducing haven demand. Gold has fallen and equities are near record levels, so the cross-asset signals that usually come with franc strength are not lined up. The SNB itself noted earlier in the year that haven demand for the franc had been limited and that low volatility made it attractive for carry. With both escalation and resolution plausible and of similar size, the factor carries no strategic direction, although the haven asymmetry means any stress episode would still go against the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Positioning on both currencies points the same way, which strengthens the signal for the pair. On the franc, CFTC data for the week to 27 October show leveraged funds net short 17,502 contracts. That is the largest net short in the 25 reports since May, and 3,895 contracts were added in the week. Asset managers are at their least-short reading in the same window at -25,067, after covering 18,241 contracts since July. Fast money therefore holds the short that would be covered first in any stress. On the Singapore dollar there is no reportable futures contract. The usable proxy is the S$NEER, which OCBC estimated at about 1.65% above its band mid-point on 15 October, down from 1.85% before the MAS hold. That leaves more room to slip towards the middle than to rise towards the strong edge. MAS reserves rose S$2.84bn in September, consistent with MAS leaning against strength. A franc short squeeze and a slip in the S$NEER both push the pair lower. The caveat is that the franc short is held mostly against the US dollar, so the read-across to this cross is indirect.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This pairs two of the largest external surpluses in the group, so the factor mostly cancels out. Singapore's current account was 16.7% of GDP in 2025, and the second-quarter 2026 surplus of S$37.08bn was 21% higher than a year earlier. Switzerland's is 9.2% of GDP, with a second-quarter surplus of CHF 23.7bn, more than double the CHF 10.2bn of a year earlier. Bilateral goods trade is small and runs against Singapore. On IMF DOTS 2024 data, Singapore exported $2.2bn to Switzerland and imported $8.1bn, a net deficit of $5.8bn. Swiss mirror data show exports of $6.5bn and imports of $3.9bn; the gap between the two reflects gold, pharma and transshipment recording. These flows are small next to each economy's total trade and largely invoiced in third currencies, so they are not a material flow for the pair. Over four weeks monthly trade data are noisy on both sides, with Swiss pharma timing and Singapore's electronics surge, and neither is likely to change the picture.

Switzerland's surplus is smaller but recovering fast, and the US tariff on Swiss goods and patented pharma is now settled at 15%. Real valuation leans the other way. The Singapore dollar's real effective rate is at the 88th percentile since January 2024, while the franc's is at a 33-month low. At the margin, competitiveness favours Swiss exporters and argues against chasing the Singapore dollar higher. GDP-based PPP says the opposite, but that gap is structural and does not close within months. With the surplus effect cancelling and real valuation a mild headwind that does not show up on this horizon, the factor is Neutral.

Bilateral investment context: the two economies compete for the same pool of mobile capital more than they trade with each other. net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Singapore is a net crude importer with a large refining and bunkering sector. Under the oil direction rules, rising oil is a mild negative for SGD (-), partly offset by refining margins that rose to about US$30 a barrel when the Hormuz disruption began.

Under the rules, rising gold is a positive for CHF (+) through the haven correlation. Gold fell 7.03% in October.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1: oil up 10% gives SGD a mild negative (-) on the import bill, partly hedged by refining. Step 2: CHF has no direct oil sensitivity in the rules, and energy is a small CPI share, so the direct effect is roughly neutral (0). An oil spike caused by conflict, however, usually comes with haven demand for the franc (+). Step 3: the net is mildly bearish for SGD/CHF on an oil rise and mildly bullish on an oil fall. Step 4: for gold, a rise gives CHF a mild positive (+) and SGD nothing, so the pair dips slightly. October's gold fall was therefore a mild support for the pair. The oil and gold moves of October roughly offset.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks spoke last in October and neither has a scheduled communication in the next four weeks. MAS's 14 October statement was a hawkish hold. It kept an appreciating slope, estimated near 1.25% a year, and said the risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. That keeps the S$NEER rising against its basket, which includes the franc, by about 0.1% a month. The SNB's 22 October summary of deliberations dropped the language about an increased willingness to intervene, removing a soft cap on franc strength. It kept the standard line that it will act in the currency market as necessary. The two signals point in opposite directions for the pair: MAS's slope is a steady tailwind for the Singapore dollar, while the SNB's retreat on intervention makes franc strength somewhat easier. Both banks are highly credible and the market accepts both messages, so the gap between guidance and pricing is near zero for each. With no event in the window, the factor is Neutral.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the factors that give each currency its own Bullish strategic verdict (external surplus, credible hawkish central bank, AAA public finances) are the same on both sides of this pair, so they cancel. External Balance carries 0.16 of the weight and scores zero: Singapore's surplus near 17% of GDP and Switzerland's near 9% both create a steady structural bid. Real valuation favours the franc at the margin, but on a timescale longer than this horizon. Fiscal is zero because both sovereigns are AAA with surpluses. What remains is carry against Swiss policy risk. Policy & Rates adds +0.110 because the roughly 130bp money-market gap should hold or widen slightly as SORA follows US rates, with the SNB likely to stay at zero on 10 December. Guidance & Credibility takes off 0.060 because that same 10 December assessment brings a new conditional forecast that the CHF dossier expects to drift hawkish. The Swiss curve does not price that, while MAS's tightening bias is already in the price and its next statement is not on the confirmed calendar. USD Liquidity takes off 0.037 because the horizon covers the year-end dollar-funding turn and the January period when franc carry positions have tended to be cut. The net is +0.014, which is Neutral. The dossiers agree, being Bullish on their own currencies by almost the same margin (+0.138 and +0.133). Priced in are an SNB on hold into mid-2027 and an unchanged MAS band. Our edge is only the hawkish SNB forecast risk, which would narrow carry from the Swiss side. Over one to three months the pair should drift sideways, earning carry, with the 10 December assessment as the one scheduled repricing point and haven episodes as the main unscheduled risk. Catalysts are the 9 December FOMC, the 10 December SNB, the 17 December ECB and the 18 December BoJ, with Singapore's next MAS statement not yet confirmed. Conviction is 1: the score is close to zero, no factor exceeds 55 confidence, and the reading is the result of offsetting strengths, not a view in waiting.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the Singapore dollar ranks 3rd of 11 in its own dossier and the franc 4th in its own, so SGD/CHF pairs two adjacent, structurally strong currencies. That makes it one of the least attractive directional pairs for either. The Singapore dossier's preferred strategic trades are short EUR/SGD and long SGD/NOK once oil stabilises. The CHF dossier prefers short EUR/CHF, short GBP/CHF and short AUD/CHF. Both are better expressed against weaker partners than against each other.

base_case.timeframe: To 29 January 2027 (1-3 months, with six-month references)
conditions: The SNB holds at 0% on 10 December and its 2027 forecast rises no further than 0.9%.
MAS keeps the slope near 1.25% a year and the S$NEER stays in the upper half of the band.
The OAT-Bund spread stays between 120bp and 170bp, with no full Hormuz closure.
The money-market gap holds at 130-150bp as SORA follows a December Fed hike.
base_case.path: SGD/CHF is flat at 0.6450 by 29 January 2027, with 21 pips of carry earned.

conditions: Target context: into the five-touch 0.65375-0.65823 band and through the 0.6550 52-week high (+111 pips, +1.72%).
A Gulf ceasefire takes Brent below US$95 and haven demand for the franc fades, with the OAT-Bund spread below 120bp.
The SNB forecast leaves 2027 inflation at 0.8% or lower, or MAS tightens slightly at its January statement.
Target context: between the two-touch 0.6284 and the 0.6375 support (-182 pips, -2.83%).
The SNB signals a 2027 hike or raises its 2027 forecast to 1.0% or higher on 10 December, narrowing the carry gap from the Swiss side.
A haven episode (OAT-Bund above 200bp, or Gulf escalation with Brent above US$130) coincides with the year-end dollar-funding squeeze on Asian dollar-hub currencies.

strategic.path_expectation: The path runs in three phases. From November to early December, a range of 0.6412-0.6507, with carry accruing and the pair held under the falling 200-week average. On 9-10 December, the Fed and SNB meetings in successive sessions are the pivot. A hawkish SNB forecast would break the pair below 0.6412 and open 0.6375, then 0.6284, over the year-end turn, when thin liquidity and dollar-funding demand amplify moves. A neutral SNB leaves the range intact. In early January, the falling 200-week average should meet an unchanged spot near 0.6450. That ends the overhead cap on its own and makes the late-January MAS statement the next decision point. Pullbacks against any rally should find buyers at the 50-day (now 0.64417, rising), and rallies should meet selling first at 0.6507, then at 0.6550-0.6582. Volatility should stay at 4.5-6%, with fat tails on the franc side.

increase_conditions: Rise to 2 (Bearish) if the 10 December SNB forecast puts 2027 inflation at 1.0% or higher, or signals a March 2027 hike; or Swiss two-year yields rise above 0.30% while the OAT-Bund spread holds above 150bp.

Rise to 2 (Bullish) if the SNB leaves its 2027 forecast at 0.8% and SORA rises above 1.45% (gap above 145bp); or MAS tightens the slope in January; or Brent falls below US$95 for ten sessions on a ceasefire. Rise to 3 (either direction) only if two of the conditions above coincide and the pair confirms on a weekly close beyond 0.6375 (Bearish) or 0.6582 (Bullish).
decrease_conditions: Stay at 1 while the SNB holds with an unchanged forecast, MAS holds, and the gap stays at 125-150bp; there is no lower rung, so conviction stays at the floor of 1.
Any shift in the SNB or MAS stance that moves the net score outside +/-0.10 would change the stance rather than lower conviction.

risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -161 pips / -2.50% (-182 pips spot plus 21 carry); upside payoff +132 pips / +2.05% (+111 plus 21)
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.61 in spot terms (111 pips upside / 182 pips downside)
risk_reward.expected_value: 0.50 x 22 + 0.25 x 132 - 0.25 x 161 = 11.0 + 33.0 - 40.25 = +4 pips. Spot alone gives 0.50 x 1 + 0.25 x 111 - 0.25 x 182 = -17 pips. Assessed for a long SGD/CHF carry position from 0.64492, earning about 21 pips over three months.
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Three months of carry almost exactly pays for the larger haven-driven downside tail, which is what a near-zero score at conviction 1 should look like. A long position is a carry harvest that needs a hard stop. A short position pays carry to own the tail.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral (score +0.053, conviction 2): carry and Singapore's data lead offset by the franc's haven bid, the leveraged franc short and the post-midterm event tail.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Neutral (score +0.014, conviction 1): carry favours the Singapore dollar, offset by unpriced hawkish SNB risk at the 10 December forecast round and year-end funding seasonality.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not measurable: no bank research publishes a forecast for this cross.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not measurable without a bank consensus.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: No bank consensus exists for SGD/CHF. The pages that appear in searches are automated extrapolation models and retail guides, not bank research, so they are not used. The closest comparison is each bank's dollar-leg forecast, but combining forecasts from different banks on different dates does not give a consensus on the cross. On fundamentals, our view differs from the two standalone dossiers in one way: each is Bullish on its own currency strategically, and we show that those Bullish drivers (surplus, credibility, fiscal strength) cancel in this pair. That leaves carry against Swiss policy risk. The research confirms that only non-bank material exists. One retail conversion guide published earlier in the year suggested SGD/CHF could recover towards 0.630-0.650 by year-end, while acknowledging the uncertainty; the pair has already reached the top of that range. A model-driven forecast page put the near-term bias at mild downside with an expected range of 0.6340-0.6450 as of mid-September, and another site states its figures are generated by a statistical model from 6,035 days of price history. None of these is research with a stated fundamental basis, and none is used as a benchmark. The scored stance stands, but our level work leans against the pair in one respect: the distribution, not the direction. Two things make the downside tail heavier than the upside: the real-valuation gap between a Singapore dollar at the 88th percentile and a franc at its lowest real rate since early 2024, and the thin support below spot set against dense resistance above it. That asymmetry does not show up in the factor scores because it is either too slow to act within the horizon (valuation) or is about levels rather than direction (structure). It is the main reason we would not hold a carry long without a stop.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If both currencies' structural strengths keep cancelling, a long SGD/CHF position earns its roughly 130bp a year of carry with little directional loss, and a short position pays that carry for nothing.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the franc's haven bid takes over through French stress or a Gulf escalation, or the SNB signals a move off zero on 10 December, the pair falls faster than carry can make up the loss. If MAS tightens again, the pair rises and a Neutral stance misses it.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Neutral, but for different reasons. Tactically, five directional factors offset each other: carry and data for the Singapore dollar against haven demand, positioning and events for the franc. Strategically, the factors that carry the most weight score zero because both currencies share them, and carry is offset by SNB forecast risk and funding seasonality. Conviction is lower strategically (1 against 2) because the near-zero score there rests on cancellation more than on tension between factors.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: There is no directional trade in the cross at either horizon. The 10 December SNB assessment is the scheduled point where the strategic balance could tip: a hawkish forecast would turn the pair Bearish and a dovish one would leave carry dominant.

Our expected path is flat spot, so the measured edge is just the carry, not a forecast of Singapore dollar appreciation. If the haven tail arrives, the downside scenario (0.6310 at three months) is 118 pips through the rate-implied three-month outright, which is why the carry edge needs a stop to remain an edge.

catalysts.rationale: September CPI was 1.0% with core at 0.5%. A print of 1.2% or more would revive SNB hike pricing for December from about 6bp, narrowing the carry gap and pushing the pair lower. A print of 0.8% or less would confirm that the franc stays at zero and help the pair through carry.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections (window for US strikes on Iran opens)
catalysts.rationale: The result opens the window in which US strikes on Iran become possible. A strike would lift oil and draw haven flows into the franc, while pulling the Singapore dollar down against the US dollar within its band, so the pair falls on both sides. A calm result with no escalation leaves the pair on carry.

Consensus is about +55k with unemployment at 4.2%. A strong print firms December Fed pricing, which lifts SORA slightly through the forward market (good for SGD carry) and weakens the franc as a funding currency. A very weak print raising recession fears would instead favour the franc's haven role.

A hot core print would lock in the December Fed hike and keep the franc in its funding role, mildly supporting the pair through carry. A soft print would bring forward the end of the Fed's hiking phase, which the CHF dossier sees moving the dollar towards the bottom of its smile, where the franc usually does better than the band-managed Singapore dollar.

catalysts.event: Singapore October NODX (week of 17 November; date unconfirmed)
catalysts.rationale: September NODX rose 68.4% y/y on a 107.6% jump in electronics. A print above +40% would reinforce the data lead behind the tactical Bullish Factor 2, while a drop below +20% would be the first sign of the AI export cycle turning. The band damps how far either outcome moves the Singapore dollar.

catalysts.event: Singapore October CPI and MAS core inflation (week of 23 November; date unconfirmed)
catalysts.rationale: Core inflation is 2.0%. A rise to 2.3% would revive talk of MAS tightening and support the pair. A print of 1.8% or lower would extend the slip in the S$NEER towards its mid-point, the second leg of the Bearish positioning read.

catalysts.event: Swiss federal votes (pension VAT funding, married-couple taxation, war-material act, fireworks)
catalysts.rationale: None of the four proposals changes the Swiss economic outlook. Approval of VAT funding for the pension system would be a small positive for fiscal sustainability, but it would not move the franc against the Singapore dollar.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00-4.25% is about 77% priced. A hike followed by a signal to pause would start the end of the Fed's hiking phase, which favours the franc. Projections showing further hikes would keep the franc a funding currency and lift SORA further, which supports the pair's carry.

catalysts.event: SNB quarterly monetary policy assessment with new conditional forecast
catalysts.rationale: This is the only decision on the confirmed calendar for either currency in the horizon. A hold is about 85% likely, but the CHF dossier expects the conditional forecast to raise 2027 inflation to 0.9-1.0%, and any hint of a 2027 hike would narrow the roughly 130bp carry gap from the Swiss side. That is not priced and would push the pair lower. Rabobank noted that the consensus view of a December SNB hike was that it was highly unlikely given Eurozone fiscal jitters and their impact on haven demand for the franc.

The ECB affects this cross through EUR/CHF. A hike that steadies euro-area sentiment would reduce the European-stress haven bid for the franc and help the pair. A decision that coincides with renewed French budget stress in December would extend that bid and weigh on the pair.

A BoJ hike to 1.50% would make the yen a higher-yielding haven than the franc by 150bp and could shift some haven demand from the franc to the yen at the margin, a mild help to the pair. The effect on this cross is second-order and largely priced.

Year-end dollar demand firms offshore funding for Asian dollar-hub currencies through the forward market, and thin liquidity amplifies franc haven moves. This is the seasonal channel behind the strategic Bearish Factor 10, and the CHF dossier expects franc firmness into January as carry positions are cut.

catalysts.event: MAS January Monetary Policy Statement (latest date)
catalysts.rationale: MAS manages the Singapore dollar against a basket, which smooths its moves without guaranteeing anything against the franc, and its next statement is due no later than 29 January 2027. The Singapore dossier weights a hold at 75%, a slight tightening at 15% and an easing at 10%. A tightening would lift the pair, an easing would push it towards the 0.6284 support.

invalidators.condition: The SNB hikes on 10 December, or its forecast puts 2027 inflation at 1.0% or higher with a signal of a March 2027 hike
invalidators.mechanism: The 130bp carry gap, the only strategic support for the pair, would narrow by 25bp or more at the same time as the haven currency gained a yield story.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SNB policy rate and conditional inflation forecast; Swiss two-year yield above 0.30%

invalidators.condition: The OAT-Bund spread closes above 170bp for five sessions with EUR/CHF below 0.9100
invalidators.mechanism: The euro-specific haven bid would force leveraged franc shorts to cover and the Singapore dollar has no matching support. A daily close below 0.6375 would confirm the break of the nearest support.

invalidators.condition: A negotiated Gulf ceasefire takes Brent below US$100 for ten sessions
invalidators.mechanism: Both pair-negative channels reverse together: Singapore's import bill and imported inflation fall, and haven demand for the franc fades.

invalidators.condition: SNB weekly domestic sight deposits rise by more than CHF 10bn over four weeks
invalidators.mechanism: Renewed franc selling by the SNB would restore the soft cap on franc strength that it withdrew in October, removing the haven tail from this cross.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SNB domestic sight deposits, from CHF 435.36bn

invalidators.condition: MAS increases the slope at its January statement
invalidators.mechanism: A faster-rising band mid-point lifts the S$NEER against a basket that includes the franc, while the SNB stays at zero, so carry and policy direction both favour the Singapore dollar.

invalidators.condition: Swiss CPI prints 0.7% or lower in October or November
invalidators.mechanism: It would remove the SNB's 2027 hike option (the strategic Bearish Factor 6), leaving the carry gap uncontested.

invalidators.condition: The S$NEER slips below 1.0% above its band mid-point, or MAS reserves fall by more than S$5bn in a month
invalidators.mechanism: Trade-weighted length would be unwinding faster than the slope can absorb, weakening the base leg against every basket currency including the franc.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Bank S$NEER estimates; MAS official reserves

signposts.indicator: French 10Y OAT less German 10Y Bund spread
signposts.confirms_if: Holds between 130bp and 170bp, so the haven bid stays contained and carry balances it
signposts.invalidates_if: Above 170bp for five sessions (Bearish) or below 120bp (Bullish)
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the franc's specific haven driver, and the Singapore dollar has no exposure to it. It moves SGD/CHF more cleanly than either USD pair, because USD/SGD barely reacts to French stress.

signposts.invalidates_if: 1.2% or higher (Bearish, reviving SNB hike pricing) or 0.7% or lower (Bullish)
signposts.bilateral_importance: Swiss inflation is the only route by which the 130bp carry gap narrows from the Swiss side, so it matters more for this positive-carry cross than for franc pairs where the gap is 250-460bp.

signposts.indicator: Estimated S$NEER position vs band mid-point
signposts.invalidates_if: Below 1.0% (Bearish) or a slope increase resets it above 1.9% (Bullish)
signposts.bilateral_importance: The franc is a basket currency in the S$NEER, so slippage within the band transmits directly to SGD/CHF. This is the base leg's equivalent of positioning data.

signposts.current_level: -17,502 contracts (week to 27 October 2026), the most short in 25 weeks
signposts.invalidates_if: Covered to above -8,000 while the franc rallies (Bearish squeeze), or extended beyond -25,000 with calm spreads (carry dominant)
signposts.bilateral_importance: The franc short is the fuel for any haven squeeze. Because the Singapore dollar has no futures positioning to offset it, the franc leg's crowding passes straight into the cross.

signposts.indicator: Three-month SORA less SNB policy rate
signposts.invalidates_if: Below 105bp (an SNB hike or SORA falling) or above 155bp (carry dominance strengthening)
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's only carry measure, since no forward exists. It is the single number behind the largest positive contribution on both horizons.

signposts.invalidates_if: Below US$100 for ten sessions (Bullish) or above US$130 on Gulf escalation (Bearish)
signposts.bilateral_importance: Oil hits Singapore's import bill and, when the move comes from conflict, bids the franc as a haven. Both effects point the pair the same way, which is not the case for either currency against the dollar.

signposts.invalidates_if: A rise of more than CHF 10bn over four weeks (renewed intervention, Bullish for the pair)
signposts.bilateral_importance: SNB intervention is the only official cap on the franc tail that hits this cross. MAS cannot provide an equivalent backstop against the franc specifically.

assumptions: Price data: the analysis uses daily closing prices for 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is SGD/CHF 0.64492 at the Friday 30 October 2026 close. The valuation date of Sunday 1 November 2026 falls on the weekend that followed, so no trading session is missing between spot and the valuation date. Weekend bars are excluded from the series, and none needed removing in this window.

Moving averages, the 200-week average and its slope, and the support and resistance zones are computed over the full history of 4,920 weekday bars from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (plus 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars). The 130 daily bars cover the 1-6 month strategic horizon and are used for the recent price-action narrative and the high/low structure.
Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 31 pips.

Zones come from clustered weekly and monthly swing closes. Their stated distances are measured from spot to the centre of each zone, and edge distances are given where they matter. The 52-week percentile is quoted on a closing basis (81st); the intraday-basis figure is 80th. The market_context 52-week range fields use the closing range.

CHF rates: the SNB policy rate of 0% is as of 27 October 2026. The Swiss ten-year yield of 0.59% in the rate data is a monthly figure as of September 2026 and is not quoted as a live level. The 0.47% figure is the 30 October daily close.

SGD rates: there is no policy-rate or ten-year series for the Singapore dollar, because MAS targets the S$NEER band rather than a rate. Three-month compounded SORA (1.297%, 30 October) is used as the Singapore short rate (entered as base_policy_rate), and the 2.24% SGS ten-year (30 October) is used for yields. No direct rate or yield differential is calculated in the rate data. The 129.7bp carry is our own SORA-minus-SNB calculation.

Implied volatility: none exists for SGD/CHF, because no Singapore dollar option is listed on any exchange. It is left blank (null), not estimated, and so are the implied-vol percentile and carry-to-vol ratio. USD/CHF implied volatility and skew are used only as qualitative leg proxies.
CFTC percentiles for the Singapore dollar and the franc are not given in the report and are left null; the Singapore dollar has no futures contract.
Forward funding: no forward funding differential exists, because the Singapore dollar has no listed future. The forward table is labelled throughout as rate-implied, not observed.
Positioning and band estimates: the S$NEER position and slope are bank model estimates (OCBC and UOB). CFTC franc positioning is against the US dollar, and its read-across to this cross is indirect.

Calendar: the confirmed decision calendar in the window contains only the SNB's 10 December assessment. The MAS January statement is dated by its latest date of 29 January 2027. Singapore data release dates are given as weeks and are unconfirmed. Dossier dates are not stated in the report; the valuation date is used for both.
Weights: Risk Appetite is raised by +0.03 on both horizons, Event Risk by +0.01 on both, and USD Liquidity cut by -0.04 on both. Each horizon sums to 1.00.

Horizons and scenarios: the tactical horizon is four weeks. Strategic factor assessments use a one-to-three-month lens, with scenarios dated to 29 January 2027 and six-month references in the forward table. Scenario probabilities are fixed at 50/25/25. Scenario targets, stops and sizing are set from the computed zones, the moving averages and ATR. No factor stance rests on this pair's trailing return, moving averages, zones or percentile, except Factor 9, whose subject is market structure.

Sources: no bank publishes an SGD/CHF forecast. The model and retail pages found are listed for completeness and not used as consensus. Bilateral goods trade uses IMF DOTS 2024 figures as supplied, and the mirror-data gap is not re-estimated.
